item.title: Installing authn-bridge
item.description:
The repository ships the unit and the user it runs as:packaging/systemd/authn-bridge.service andpackaging/sysusers.d/authn-bridge.conf. Everything below runs as root unless it says otherwise.
/usr/local/bin/authn-bridge the binary
/etc/authn-bridge/*.hcl the configuration, read in name order; root:authn-bridge, 0750, files 0640
/var/lib/authn-bridge/ keys, the subject salt, the SQLite state, the certificates issued, the disabled list; authn-bridge, 0700
/run/authn-bridge/ the admin socket, when the configuration asks for one

The binary

A release carries authn-bridge-<os>-<arch> for Linux, macOS and Windows on amd64 and arm64, a SHA256SUMS manifest and a build provenance attestation per binary; verifying a download says how to check both. Or build it, which records the version in the binary:

$ go install github.com/go-authn/bridge/cmd/authn-bridge@v0.23.3
$ authn-bridge --version
authn-bridge version v0.23.3

The path matters: from v0.20.0 the program lives in internal/app and the command in cmd/authn-bridge, so go install github.com/go-authn/bridge@... builds nothing.

The user, and why it is not a dynamic one 

install -m 0755 authn-bridge-linux-amd64 /usr/local/bin/authn-bridge
install -D -m 0644 authn-bridge.conf /etc/sysusers.d/authn-bridge.conf
systemd-sysusers # creates the authn-bridge user and group
install -m 0644 authn-bridge.service /etc/systemd/system/authn-bridge.service
systemctl daemon-reload

install -d -m 0750 -o root -g authn-bridge /etc/authn-bridge
install -d -m 0700 -o authn-bridge -g authn-bridge /var/lib/authn-bridge

The unit names User=authn-bridge, not DynamicUser=. The signing key, the subject salt, the SAML key and the certificate authorities are made before the first start, live for years, and must keep one owner across reinstalls and restores from backup. A dynamic user gets its UID when the service starts.

The keys

Run keygen as the service’s user, so that it owns what it writes. It refuses to overwrite a file that is already there:

$ mkdir var/nfs-ca
$ authn-bridge keygen --key var/oidc.key --salt var/salt --ssh-ca var/ssh-ca --x509-ca var/nfs-ca
wrote var/ssh-ca; its public half, for go-fileshare's trusted_user_ca_file:
ssh-ed25519 AAAAC3NzaC1lZDI1NTE5AAAAIBNOYvUrAPdRTB+38aml+twPN+2k1shD3l62v8NxrIje go-authn-bridge-ca
wrote var/oidc.key
wrote var/nfs-ca/ca.crt and its key; the certificate is what go-fileshare trusts for NFS over TLS
wrote var/salt -- keep it: a new salt is a new subject for everybody
$ authn-bridge keygen --key var/oidc.key
authn-bridge: open var/oidc.key: file exists

On a server the paths are under /var/lib/authn-bridge, and the command isrunuser -u authn-bridge -- authn-bridge keygen ....

flag writes for
--key an RSA 3072 key ID tokens (RS256), published at /jwks
--salt 32 random bytes every sub, which is an HMAC under it
--access-token-key a P-256 key access tokens signed ES256 instead, much shorter
--ssh-ca an Ed25519 key in OpenSSH format the SSH certificates and the KRL’s signature
--x509-ca DIR DIR/ca.key (P-256) and DIR/ca.crt, valid ten years, path length 0 NFS client certificates and the CRL

Back up the salt, and never change it

A new salt gives every person a new sub, and every relying party then sees a new person. The same goes for deleting it on uninstall.

The SAML key and certificate are made with openssl: they are what the federation registers and what every IdP encrypts to. The key must be RSA (IdPs encrypt to it with RSA-OAEP). It is not the TLS certificate, and does not change with it.

runuser -u authn-bridge -- sh -c 'umask 077; openssl req -x509 -newkey rsa:3072 -nodes -days 3650 \
 -subj "/CN=login.example.org" \
 -keyout /var/lib/authn-bridge/saml.key -out /var/lib/authn-bridge/saml.crt'

The federation’s metadata signing certificate comes from the federation, and so does its SHA-256 fingerprint: take the fingerprint from the federation’s web page, never from the same download as the certificate. Seethe federation side.

The unit

What it grants, in short:

  • Type=exec, Restart=on-failure, RestartSec=5s, TimeoutStopSec=20s.The provider shuts its listener down within ten seconds of SIGTERM.
  • StateDirectory=, RuntimeDirectory= (both 0700) andConfigurationDirectory= (0750), UMask=0077. WithProtectSystem=strict, everything else is read-only.
  • No capability (CapabilityBoundingSet= and AmbientCapabilities= empty),NoNewPrivileges=, PrivateUsers=, PrivateTmp=, PrivateDevices=,PrivateIPC=, ProtectHome=, the kernel, clock, hostname and control groups protected.
  • RestrictAddressFamilies=AF_UNIX AF_INET AF_INET6: TCP for the listener,the metadata, an ACME CA and a database; a socket for the admin API.
  • SystemCallFilter=@system-service, minus @privileged @resources, refused with EPERM rather than a kill.

It waits for network-online.target, because the metadata is fetched before the provider listens.

systemctl enable --now authn-bridge
journalctl -u authn-bridge -n 20

The first line in the journal is the one shown onthe overview.

Changes need a restart

The configuration is read once. The unit has no ExecReload=, so systemctl reload is refused rather than pretending. A SIGHUP (from logrotate, or habit)is caught, logged and ignored. Left to Go’s default it would kill the process,and systemd would count that as a clean exit that Restart=on-failure does not restart:

SIGHUP: ignored, nothing is reloaded; restart the service to apply a configuration change (TLS certificate files are re-read on their own)

TLS certificate files are the exception: they are re-read when they change.

Port 443

The default listener is 127.0.0.1:8080, behind a TLS reverse proxy, and needs no capability. To serve TLS itself on port 443 (cert_file or acme),the provider needs CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE and must leave the private user namespace, since a capability held inside it does not apply to the host’s network:

# /etc/systemd/system/authn-bridge.service.d/port-443.conf
[Service]
CapabilityBoundingSet=CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE
AmbientCapabilities=CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE
PrivateUsers=no

Upgrading, and going back

Back up /var/lib/authn-bridge first: it holds the keys and the salt, which cannot be made again. Keep the binary that works, install the new one, restart:

cp -p /usr/local/bin/authn-bridge /usr/local/bin/authn-bridge.previous
install -m 0755 authn-bridge-linux-amd64 /usr/local/bin/authn-bridge
systemctl restart authn-bridge

Going back is the same with authn-bridge.previous. A newer release may ship a newer unit: compare it with yours, install it and systemctl daemon-reload before the restart.

Coming from bridge

The configuration is unchanged; only the command and the release assets were renamed. Change every unit, script, cron job and bearer_token_command that runs bridge. The log line and the error prefix now say authn-bridge, so an alert that matched bridge v0. must match authn-bridge v0.. Metric names(bridge_*), the bridge_state table and the user-side cache(go-authn-bridge in the user’s configuration directory, ~/.config on Linux) are unchanged, so authn-bridge token reuses the logins bridge cached.

item.title: Installing authn-revokd
item.description:
The repository ships three units and an account in packaging/:authn-revokd.service (the daemon), authn-revokd-once.service withauthn-revokd-once.timer (the alternative), andsysusers.d/authn-revokd.conf.

path what owner, mode
/usr/local/bin/authn-revokd the binary root, 0755
/usr/lib/sysusers.d/authn-revokd.conf the authn-revokd system account root, 0644
/etc/systemd/system/authn-revokd.service the daemon root, 0644
/etc/authn-revokd/revokd.hcl the configuration, the default -config root, 0644
/etc/authn-revokd/ca/ the CA keys and certificates the lists must be signed by root, 0755; the files in it 0644
/var/lib/authn-revokd/ StateDirectory=, the only writable place authn-revokd, 0755
/var/lib/authn-revokd/state/ state_dir: the verified copies authn-revokd, 0700
/var/lib/authn-revokd/sshd.krl an output: what sshd reads authn-revokd, 0644

Write the outputs to /var/lib/authn-revokd, and point the servers there. An output is written beside its final name and renamed over it, so itsdirectory must be writable. Making /etc/ssh writable would let theauthn-revokd account replace sshd_config. Outputs are 0644, chmod-ed explicitly despite UMask=0077, so that sshd and a TLS server running as its own user can read them; the state stays 0700.

The binary, the account, the unit

A release carries authn-revokd-<os>-<arch> for Linux, macOS and Windows on amd64 and arm64, with SHA256SUMS and build provenance(verifying a download). Orgo install github.com/go-authn/revocation/cmd/authn-revokd@v0.6.5.

The account and the unit come from the packaging/ directory of the release tag, the same version as the binary: copy that directory beside the binary,from a checkout of the tag or, for v0.6.5, fromhttps://github.com/go-authn/revocation/tree/v0.6.5/packaging.

install -m 0755 authn-revokd-linux-amd64 /usr/local/bin/authn-revokd
install -m 0644 packaging/sysusers.d/authn-revokd.conf /usr/lib/sysusers.d/authn-revokd.conf
systemd-sysusers /usr/lib/sysusers.d/authn-revokd.conf
install -m 0644 packaging/systemd/authn-revokd.service /etc/systemd/system/
systemctl daemon-reload

The account is static, not DynamicUser=. authn-revokd refuses a state directory owned by anyone but its own uid or root, and the state must keep ordering the next list across restarts and upgrades. With a dynamic user the files would sit under /var/lib/private, 0700 root, and a TLS server running as its own user could not read the CRL.

The daemon 

[Service]
Type=exec
ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/authn-revokd -config /etc/authn-revokd/revokd.hcl
ExecReload=/bin/kill -HUP $MAINPID
Restart=always

and around it: User=authn-revokd, no capability at all, NoNewPrivileges=,ProtectSystem=strict with StateDirectory=authn-revokd (0755) the one writable place, PrivateUsers=, PrivateTmp=, PrivateDevices=,PrivateIPC=, AF_INET AF_INET6 AF_UNIX only, @system-service system calls minus @privileged @resources.

Restart=always, because sshd ignores the expiry in the KRL. The file is failed closed by this process when a list lapses. While it is stopped, sshd keeps reading the last file it wrote, and a revocation issued meanwhile never arrives. Monitor the unit, or /healthz when the mirror is on.

systemctl reload syncs now. It sends SIGHUP, and the agent fetches every source at once instead of at the next refresh:

hangup: syncing now

It does not re-read the configuration, which is read once, at start: after changing revokd.hcl, systemctl restart authn-revokd. (Before v0.6.0 an uncaught SIGHUP killed the process, and systemd counts that as a clean exit.)

Enable it BEFORE wiring sshd

sshd refuses every certificate when RevokedKeys names a file that does not exist

So start authn-revokd first, and wait until the output is there:ssh-keygen -Q -l -f /var/lib/authn-revokd/sshd.krl prints its comment,authn-revokd sshd while every source is current.

systemctl enable --now authn-revokd
journalctl -u authn-revokd -n 20 # "<source>: version N, issued ..., expires ..."
 # "output sshd: wrote /var/lib/authn-revokd/sshd.krl"

Then, in /etc/ssh/sshd_config:

TrustedUserCAKeys /etc/ssh/ca/univ-a-ssh.pub
RevokedKeys /var/lib/authn-revokd/sshd.krl

and sshd -t && systemctl reload ssh. sshd reads RevokedKeys at every authentication, so it needs no reload when authn-revokd rewrites the file: the atomic rename is enough.

A TLS server’s CRL 

ssl_client_certificate /etc/authn-revokd/ca/univ-a-x509.pem;
ssl_verify_client on;
ssl_crl /var/lib/authn-revokd/univ-a.crl; # format = "pem"

A TLS server reads its CRL when it loads its configuration, so it must be reloaded when the file changes. An on_change command runs as theauthn-revokd account, which cannot systemctl reload nginx: let systemd watch the file instead, as root, with a path unit (PathChanged= on the output) that starts a oneshot running systemctl reload nginx.

Or: -once, on a timer

authn-revokd -once syncs once and exits, 1 when a list is not current or could not be fetched (what -once reports).The outputs are written either way, and failed closed for sshd once a list lapses.

# authn-revokd-once.service
[Unit]
Conflicts=authn-revokd.service

[Service]
Type=oneshot
ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/authn-revokd -config /etc/authn-revokd/revokd.hcl -once
TimeoutStartSec=5min
# authn-revokd-once.timer
[Unit]
Conflicts=authn-revokd.service

[Timer]
OnBootSec=30s
OnUnitActiveSec=1min
AccuracySec=5s
RandomizedDelaySec=10s

[Install]
WantedBy=timers.target

The one-shot has the daemon’s account and hardening. TimeoutStartSec=5min keeps a sync that hangs on a source from outliving the next tick, andRandomizedDelaySec=10s keeps a fleet started together from polling its issuer in step.

install -m 0644 authn-revokd-once.service authn-revokd-once.timer /etc/systemd/system/
systemctl daemon-reload
systemctl disable --now authn-revokd
systemctl enable --now authn-revokd-once.timer

Never enable both: the units conflict, so starting one stops the other.The daemon remains the better choice. It fails a lapsed list closed at its nextrefresh, where the timer waits for its next tick, and only the daemon serves as a mirror: listen is ignored with -once. A timer that stops firing is a daemon that stopped, so monitor systemctl status authn-revokd-once.

Upgrading, and going back

Install the new binary beside the old, swap, restart. The state carries over:the verified copies keep ordering the next lists, so neither an upgrade nor a rollback to an older binary lets an older list in.

Uninstalling

Remove RevokedKeys and ssl_crl from the servers’ configuration first,and reload them: sshd refuses every certificate once the file is gone.

item.title: Installing authnd
item.description:
The repository carries the two files a systemd host needs:packaging/sysusers.d/authnd.conf (the account) andpackaging/systemd/authnd.service (the unit). This page explains both and the steps around them. go-pkgx’s versioned services are meant to do this for you later; they do not exist yet.

The release binary

Each tag publishes authnd-<os>-<arch> for linux, darwin and windows on amd64 and arm64 (.exe on windows), built with CGO_ENABLED=0, a SHA256SUMS manifest, and a build provenance attestation for every binary.

version=v0.12.0
arch=amd64 # or arm64
base=https://github.com/go-authn/authnd/releases/download/$version

curl -fsSLO "$base/authnd-linux-$arch"
curl -fsSLO "$base/SHA256SUMS"

sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS --ignore-missing # the bytes the release published
gh attestation verify "authnd-linux-$arch" --repo go-authn/authnd # built by the release workflow, at that tag

Stop if either check fails. The release workflow refuses to publish a binary that does not report exactly the tag it is published under, so the version is something to compare:

$ authnd --version
authnd version v0.12.0

Building only what you want

The server is always there; two build tags leave out where people can come from. -tags nosql drops the three database drivers (PostgreSQL through pgx,MySQL/MariaDB, SQLite through modernc.org/sqlite) and the users "sql" block;-tags noldap drops the LDAP client and the users "ldap" block. A configuration naming a block the binary was built without is told so —this binary was built without SQL support (-tags nosql) — rather than that the block does not exist. The release binaries are built without tags.

The account 

#Type Name ID Description Home Shell
u authnd - "authnd LDAP directory and Kerberos KDC" /var/lib/authnd -

A static account from sysusers.d, not DynamicUser=. The files authnd reads — password files, a DSN, a keytab, a TLS key — are secrets given to theauthnd group ahead of time, and a password change writes back into them. A dynamic uid does not exist until the service starts,and a file it wrote would belong to a number that later means somebody else.

The two files come from the packaging/ directory of the release tag, the same version as the binary: copy that directory beside the binary, from a checkout of the tag or, for v0.12.0, fromhttps://github.com/go-authn/authnd/tree/v0.12.0/packaging.

sudo install -m 0755 "authnd-linux-$arch" /usr/local/bin/authnd
sudo install -m 0644 packaging/sysusers.d/authnd.conf /usr/lib/sysusers.d/authnd.conf
sudo systemd-sysusers /usr/lib/sysusers.d/authnd.conf
sudo install -m 0644 packaging/systemd/authnd.service /etc/systemd/system/authnd.service
sudo systemd-analyze verify /etc/systemd/system/authnd.service
sudo systemctl daemon-reload

What the unit grants, and why 

[Service]
Type=exec
ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/authnd --config /etc/authnd
Restart=on-failure
RestartSec=5s

User=authnd
Group=authnd
UMask=0077

AmbientCapabilities=CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE
CapabilityBoundingSet=CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE
NoNewPrivileges=yes

StateDirectory=authnd
StateDirectoryMode=0700

ProtectSystem=strict

The rest of the unit is the usual hardening (ProtectHome, PrivateTmp,PrivateDevices, ProtectProc=invisible, the kernel and cgroup protections,MemoryDenyWriteExecute, SystemCallFilter=@system-service,RestrictAddressFamilies=AF_INET AF_INET6 AF_UNIX). Three things itleaves out are deliberate:
ExecReload= authnd has no reload. It reads its configuration, certificate and keytab once; see running it
PrivateUsers= inside a user namespace CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE no longer applies to the host’s network, and the bind to 389 is refused
ProcSubset=pid it hides /proc/sys, where Go reads net/core/somaxconn, and every listener’s backlog falls to Go’s fallback of 128

IPAddressAllow=/IPAddressDeny= are not set either: which networks may ask a directory is the site’s to say, in a drop-in:

sudo systemctl edit authnd
[Service]
IPAddressDeny=any
IPAddressAllow=localhost 10.0.0.0/8

The one capability is for the privileged ports: LDAP 389, LDAPS 636, and Kerberos 88 over UDP and TCP. A PostgreSQL or MariaDB on the same machine is reached through its socket, which a read-only file system allows. The state directory, /var/lib/authnd, is there for a SQLite database; authnd keeps no state of its own — the second-factor lockout counts live in memory and are reset at every restart.

The configuration directory 

sudo install -d -o root -g authnd -m 0750 /etc/authnd

Every file inside it root:authnd, mode 0640. Secrets go in files named by*_file keys rather than inline: a file has permissions, and a configuration someone pastes does not. With ProtectSystem=strict the service cannot write under /etc, which is right for the configuration and wrong for the passwords people change themselves — give those a directory of their own:

sudo install -d -o authnd -g authnd -m 0700 /etc/authnd/passwords
sudo systemctl edit authnd
[Service]
ReadWritePaths=/etc/authnd/passwords

Why that directory and not the file is explained inchanging a password.

key default
base_dn — (required) the root of the tree, e.g. dc=example,dc=org; a value with no = is refused
listen 127.0.0.1:3893 one address. Loopback by default: a directory that appears on every interface the moment it starts is a decision somebody should make on purpose. A site that needs LDAP and LDAPS runs two instances
reader "<dn>" none a service account that may search; see who may read
cert_file, key_file, starttls, publish_nt_hash, samba off TLS
user, group, users — the people; at least one user or users block
kerberos none a realm
mfa none a second factor
oidc none a token at the bind

A relative path in the configuration is resolved against the directory the process runs in, not the configuration file’s; the unit runs from /, so write paths absolute.

Before every start:

sudo -u authnd authnd check /etc/authnd
sudo systemctl enable --now authnd
journalctl -u authnd

check is described on its own page;running it as authnd also proves the account can read every file.

Upgrade, roll back, remove

Check the configuration with the new binary before it replaces the old one, and keep the old one. The new binary is installed beside the old one first: that makes it executable, and puts it where the authnd account can run it.

sudo install -m 0755 "authnd-linux-$arch" /usr/local/bin/authnd.new
sudo -u authnd /usr/local/bin/authnd.new check /etc/authnd
sudo cp /usr/local/bin/authnd /usr/local/bin/authnd.previous
sudo mv /usr/local/bin/authnd.new /usr/local/bin/authnd
sudo systemctl restart authnd
authnd --version

Compare packaging/ at the new tag with what is installed (v0.12.0’s is v0.11.1’s, unchanged). Rolling back is the same install fromauthnd.previous, and a restart.

From v0.10.x to v0.11.0 the check above is the step that matters: a configuration with publish_nt_hash = true and nosamba block is refused there rather than at the restart, and the lines after its tables say who is no longer a posixAccount and which groups are no longer posixGroups(the entries).

⛔ From v0.11.1 to v0.12.0, upgrade whatever else you do: v0.11.1’s release binaries were built with Go 1.27.2 and are affected by GO-2026-6809(crypto/x509), which v0.12.0, built with Go 1.27.3, is not. The configuration needs no change; to serve a site’s own schema, seesite schemas, and name the files by absolute paths, since a systemd unit’s working directory is /.

To remove it:

sudo systemctl disable --now authnd
sudo rm /etc/systemd/system/authnd.service
sudo rm -r /etc/systemd/system/authnd.service.d # if a drop-in was added
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo rm /usr/local/bin/authnd /usr/local/bin/authnd.previous /usr/lib/sysusers.d/authnd.conf

/etc/authnd, /var/lib/authnd and the authnd account are left in place:the first two hold people’s credentials, and a uid that is reused can be given somebody else’s files. Remove them deliberately.

item.title: Running it: signals, restarts and what it says
item.description:
It reads everything once

The configuration files, every source behind them, the TLS certificate and the keytab are read at start. There is no reload, and the packaged unit has no ExecReload=. After changing any of them:

sudo -u authnd authnd check /etc/authnd
sudo systemctl restart authnd

The one thing applied while it runs is apassword a person changes through authnd,which re-reads the user blocks and nothing else.

Signals

signal what happens
SIGTERM, SIGINT it prints stopping, closes the listeners and every established connection, stops the realm, closes the sources, and exits 0 once the server has really finished
SIGHUP it is caught and logged, and authnd stays up without reloading anything 
$ authnd --config etc/authnd
ldap on 127.0.0.1:3893, serving 4 people from the configuration file, then a sqlite database
hangup: authnd does not reload; restart it to apply a changed configuration, certificate or keytab
alice's password change was refused: the old password did not verify: directory: wrong password
alice changed their own password
stopping

That is one run: a kill -HUP, two attempts to change a password (the first refused, the second accepted), then a kill -TERM.The process was still there after the SIGHUP.

A SIGHUP used to kill authnd — Go’s default for a signal nobody handles— and systemd counts death by SIGHUP as a clean exit, soRestart=on-failure did not start it again: one kill -HUP or one logrotatepostrotate took a directory down for good. It is caught now so that the habit is harmless, and the line says what to do instead.

Closing established connections, not only the listener, is deliberate: a server that stopped accepting and left its open connections answering would look stopped and not be, which is the restart that does not take.

What it writes

Everything goes to standard output, which under systemd is the journal(journalctl -u authnd):

  • at start, where it listens and whom it serves — ldap on …, ldaps on … or ldap+starttls on …, then realm EXAMPLE.ORG on … (udp and tcp) with akerberos block;
  • every refused bind under an mfa block, every refused token, every refused or completed password change, with the reason — which the client is never told; see the second factor and tokens;
  • every request the KDC refuses, prefixed kerberos:, with the Kerberos error code; see the realm;
  • the LDAP library’s own log, in slog text form, at level info.

A plain wrong password on a simple bind, with no mfa block, is answeredinvalidCredentials and not logged by authnd itself.

When it does not start

A refusal is one line on standard error, prefixed authnd:, and exit status 1; under the unit, Restart=on-failure then tries again every five seconds and the line is in the journal each time. Everything check refuses is refused here too, and the one thing only the server finds is an address it cannot listen on — seecheck.The LDAP listener, the certificate and the realm are all opened before the first line is printed, so a server that cannot start prints only the refusal. Here a second instance meets the first one’s Kerberos port:

$ authnd --config cases/realm2
authnd: kerberos udp 127.0.0.1:18388: listen udp 127.0.0.1:18388: bind: address already in use

The ldap on … line, and realm … on … after it, mean both halves are listening.

Telling that it is up

There is no health endpoint and no metrics. What there is:

  • the process and its exit status — under systemd, systemctl is-active authnd. If the LDAP listener or the realm stops of its own accord, the whole process ends with that error, so a live process is one whose two halves both answer;
  • the root DSE, which answers an anonymous client and says which version it is talking to:
$ ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://127.0.0.1:3893 -s base -b '' '+' '*'
dn:
objectClass: top
objectClass: OpenLDAProotDSE
supportedLDAPVersion: 3
namingContexts: dc=example,dc=org
supportedExtension: 1.3.6.1.4.1.4203.1.11.3
supportedExtension: 1.3.6.1.4.1.4203.1.11.1
supportedControl: 1.2.840.113556.1.4.319
supportedControl: 1.3.6.1.1.13.1
supportedControl: 1.3.6.1.1.13.2
supportedFeatures: 1.3.6.1.4.1.4203.1.5.1
supportedFeatures: 1.3.6.1.4.1.4203.1.5.3
subschemaSubentry: cn=Subschema
vendorName: go-authn/authnd
vendorVersion: v0.12.0

On a StartTLS listener that query needs -ZZ. A probe that proves more — that a source still answers — is a bind as a person or a reader kept for the purpose; with ausers "ldap" block, that bind reaches the directory behind this one.

What lives where, and what a restart loses

configuration, passwords, DSN, certificate, keytab the files the configuration names; nothing is copied
a SQLite database wherever its DSN says; /var/lib/authnd under the unit
second-factor counts and lockouts memory only: a restart forgets them, including a person locked out after a hundred wrong codes
used one-time codes memory only
